In late June 1950, North Korean forces crossed into South Korea. Within weeks,
American newspapers and business magazines were reporting plans for a large and
lasting rise in military spending. Ramey's narrative series prices such reports
as the change in the expected [present value]{.footnote-term
data-index="present value"}^[The present value of a stream of future spending is
its sum after each year's amount has been discounted back to the present. A
report that raises planned spending for the next three years moves the present
value at once, even though the spending itself arrives later.] of government
spending [@ramey2011]. For the third quarter of 1950 it records news worth 179.4
billion dollars, which is 0.600 of the previous quarter's nominal
[trend GDP]{.footnote-term data-index="trend GDP"}^[Ramey and Zubairy call the
series potential GDP and estimate it as a sixth-degree polynomial trend in real
GDP. The fit runs over 1889Q1–2015Q4 and leaves out 1930Q1–1946Q4, the Great
Depression and World War II; in their workbook the series is `rgdp_pott6`. It is multiplied by
the GDP deflator when a nominal value is needed. Lecture 2 explains why dividing
output and spending by trend GDP puts them in common units.] at an annual rate
[@rameyzubairy2018]. A policymaker reading
those reports would want to know what the buildup would do to output over the
next three years.

The path that followed is easy to read. Real GDP stood 2.75 percent below trend
in 1950Q2 and 5.12 percent above it in 1953Q1, ten quarters after the news
arrived: a rise of 7.87 points of trend GDP. It is tempting to call those 7.87
points the effect of the news. Many other things happened in the same quarters,
though. Taxes rose; in the postwar tax record assembled by @romerromer2010, the
largest increases motivated by spending came during the Korean War. The March
1951 [Treasury–Federal Reserve Accord]{.footnote-term
data-index="Treasury–Federal Reserve Accord"}^[The agreement that ended the
Federal Reserve's wartime commitment to peg the prices of government bonds,
leaving it free to let interest rates rise [@hetzelleach2001].] freed monetary
policy. Wage and price controls were imposed in January 1951 and dismantled
early in 1953 [@rockoff1984]. The rise of 7.87 points mixes the news with all of
these.

So the question is not what happened next. It is what happened *because of* the
news, and answering it requires a path nobody observed: the one GDP would have
followed had the news not arrived, with everything else as it was. This lecture
turns that comparison into a regression. We start in an economy small enough
that the unobserved path can be computed exactly and derive a regression whose
coefficient recovers the comparison there. Then we build that regression's rows
by hand and return to the quarterly data with one estimated response and a list
of what it has not yet earned.

By the end of the lecture, you should be able to:

1. define the causal response at horizon $h$ as the gap between the realized
   path and the path without the intervention, and distinguish it from the
   change since the date before the intervention;
2. iterate $y_t=\rho y_{t-1}+\theta_0 s_t+v_t$ forward to derive
   $\theta_h=\theta_0\rho^h$, and show that the horizon-$h$ regression of
   $y_{t+h}$ on a constant, $s_t$, and $y_{t-1}$ has $\beta_h=\theta_h$,
   $\gamma_h=\rho^{h+1}$, and a residual built from disturbances dated $t$
   through $t+h$ and shocks dated $t+1$ through $t+h$;
3. build the regression rows for $h=0,1,2$ by hand, state $T_h=T-h-p$, and
   compute $\hat\beta_h$ from those rows;
4. estimate $\hat\beta_h$ for $h=0,\dots,H$ in a Stata loop that stores
   $\hat\beta_h$ and $T_h$, and draw a response graph whose caption names the
   intervention, the units, and the counterfactual; and
5. explain what one estimated coefficient measures and where its variation
   comes from, why a single episode cannot identify it, and which claims a
   first data application has not yet earned.

The lecture assumes ordinary least squares (the slope as a covariance over a
variance, and the slope on a 0–1 regressor as a difference in means),
expectation and independence, and elementary Stata: `tsset`, time-series
operators, loops, `regress`, and stored results. No time-series course is
assumed; the one autoregression we need is built from scratch and iterated by
hand. Standard errors, instruments, and vector autoregressions come later.

## The Question: An Intervention, an Outcome, and a Path We Never See {#sec-l01-question}

The Korean episode has three parts that recur in every problem of this course.
Something happens at a date: news arrives, a policy rate moves, a state changes
its banking law. An outcome is measured at that date and afterwards. And the
question compares that outcome with what it would otherwise have been. The
first two parts can be measured. The third cannot, and an economy small enough
to compute by hand shows why no single observed path supplies it.

### Intervention, Outcome, and Two Paths

Write $s_t$ for the
[**intervention variable**]{.glossary-term data-term="intervention-variable"}
dated $t$ and $y_t$ for the outcome. In the opening, $s_t$ is a quarter's
military news measured as a fraction of trend GDP, and $y_t$ is real GDP divided
by trend GDP. The name is deliberately neutral. Calling $s_t$ a shock would
claim that nothing else systematically moves with it, and that claim needs an
argument, which Lecture 3 supplies. Until then $s_t$ is simply the variable
whose effect we want.

The data record one sequence of outcomes, the
[**realized path**]{.glossary-term data-term="realized-path"}. It carries the
effect of $s_t$ together with the effect of every other disturbance that arrived
before and after. The [**counterfactual**]{.glossary-term
data-term="counterfactual"} path, written $y^{c}_t$, is the sequence the same
economy would have produced without the intervention at date $t$ and with every
other disturbance exactly as it was. The superscript $c$ marks counterfactual
objects throughout the course. Nobody observes $y^{c}_t$.

The [**causal response**]{.glossary-term data-term="causal-response"} $h$
periods after the intervention is the gap between the two paths at the same
date:

$$
\theta_h=y_{t+h}-y^{c}_{t+h}.
$$ {#eq-l01-causal-response}

Read @eq-l01-causal-response across, not down the calendar. Both terms are
dated $t+h$, so the equation compares two versions of one period, not one period
with an earlier one. The units of $\theta_h$ are the units of $y$; when the
intervention is a one-unit change in $s_t$, they are units of $y$ per unit of
$s$. In the Korean example the gap would be measured in points of trend GDP.
The response carries no date subscript here because, in the economies of this
lecture, the gap does not depend on when the intervention arrives;
@sec-l01-two-clocks and @sec-l01-smallest-model show why. This is the sense in
which @stockwatson2018 define dynamic causal effects in macroeconomics: a
comparison of the outcomes that would follow different values of the
intervention, not a description of what followed the one value that occurred.

### The Change Since the Date Before

The number the opening read off the data was a different object: the change in
the realized path since the period before the news, $y_{t+h}-y_{t-1}$. To see
how it relates to $\theta_h$, add and subtract $y^{c}_{t+h}$:

$$
y_{t+h}-y_{t-1}
=\underbrace{\bigl(y_{t+h}-y^{c}_{t+h}\bigr)}_{\theta_h}
+\underbrace{\bigl(y^{c}_{t+h}-y_{t-1}\bigr)}_{\text{change without the intervention}}.
$$ {#eq-l01-change-decomposition}

The first bracket is the causal response. The second is the change the economy
would have made anyway, driven by everything except the intervention. The left
side of @eq-l01-change-decomposition equals $\theta_h$ only when the second
bracket is zero, that is, only when the counterfactual path would have stayed at
its pre-intervention level. Nothing guarantees that. A wartime economy with
rising taxes, a newly independent central bank, and price controls had many
reasons to move.

The decomposition relies on one fact about timing. An intervention at $t$
cannot change $y_{t-1}$, so the realized and counterfactual paths coincide
before $t$ and the same $y_{t-1}$ appears in both brackets. If people act on
news before it is recorded, that fact fails; Lecture 3 treats the consequences
under the name of anticipation.

### A Twelve-Period Economy Where the Counterfactual Is Known

To watch the two objects diverge with actual numbers, we need an economy in
which the counterfactual can be computed. Take twelve periods and the rule

$$
y_t=0.5\,y_{t-1}+s_t+v_t,\qquad t=1,\dots,12,\qquad y_0=0.
$$

Each period's outcome is half of the previous outcome, plus the intervention,
plus a [disturbance]{.footnote-term data-index="disturbance"}^[A disturbance is a
random term that stands for everything moving the outcome other than the
variables written in the equation. In a simulation the computer draws it; in
data it is whatever the model leaves out.] $v_t$ that stands for everything
else. The intervention is binary: $s_t=1$ in a period when it occurs and $0$
otherwise. Both inputs were drawn once in Stata with
[seed]{.footnote-term data-index="random-number seed"}^[A seed fixes the
starting point of Stata's pseudo-random number generator, so the same commands
reproduce the same draws on every run. The course fixes each seed before
looking at any result and keeps the draw it produces.] 1. Each $v_t$ is a
standard normal draw rounded to one decimal, and each $s_t$ is an independent
draw equal to one with probability 0.3. The interventions happen to fall at
$t=1,5,10,12$. @sec-l01-smallest-model returns to this rule with general
coefficients; here it only has to generate numbers.

<!-- D32: binary intervention, so every slope in the hand calculations is a
     difference in means; seed 1 was fixed before any result was seen. -->

@tbl-l01-hand-table lists the draws and the realized path. To build the
counterfactual for the intervention at $t=5$, set $s_5=0$, hold every $v_t$ at
its drawn value, and run the rule again.

|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1 | 0.9 | 1.9000 | 1.9000 | 0 | — |
| 2 | 0 | 0.5 | 1.4500 | 1.4500 | 0 | — |
| 3 | 0 | 0.6 | 1.3250 | 1.3250 | 0 | — |

Outcome columns are displayed to four decimals with ties rounded away from zero; the gap column is exact, and every calculation in the notes uses exact values. {#tbl-l01-hand-table}

Before period 5 the two paths are identical, as the timing argument requires.
At $t=5$ the realized outcome is $y_5=0.5(0.0625)+1-1.7=-0.66875$, while the
counterfactual is $y^{c}_5=0.5(0.0625)+0-1.7=-1.66875$. The gap is exactly one:
the intervention added one unit. Yet the realized outcome *fell* by 0.73125 from
$y_4=0.0625$, because a disturbance of $-1.7$ arrived in the same period.

From then on the gap halves every period. At $t=6$ both paths carry forward half
of their own previous value and receive the same $v_6=0.2$, so the only
difference left is half of the previous gap, $0.5\times1=0.5$. At $t=7$ the gap
is 0.25 and at $t=8$ it is 0.125. The change since $t=4$ behaves erratically by
comparison: $-0.196875$, then $1.9703125$, then $-0.34609375$.
@fig-l01-realized-counterfactual shows both comparisons.

[Two paths, one gap]{.smallcaps}. The causal response to the $t=5$ intervention is the vertical distance between the realized and counterfactual paths at the same date: 1, 0.5, 0.25, and 0.125 at $t=5,\dots,8$. The change from the pre-intervention value $y_4$ is a different quantity, $-0.731$ at $t=5$ and $1.970$ at $t=7$, because it also contains every disturbance that arrived after $t=4$.
:::

@eq-l01-change-decomposition accounts for the difference exactly. At $t=7$ the
realized change of 1.9703125 splits into the causal response 0.25 and a
counterfactual change $y^{c}_7-y_4=1.7828125-0.0625=1.7203125$, which the
disturbance $v_7=2.1$ more than accounts for. Reading the realized change as the
effect would overstate the effect nearly eightfold at $t=7$ and get its sign
wrong at $t=5$.
[Exercise 1](#exercise-l01-1) rebuilds the counterfactual path by hand.

Two features of the example will be needed again. First, the gaps
1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 do not depend on any $v_t$. Change the disturbances and the
realized path moves, but the gap sequence does not. Second, the gaps were
computable only because we knew the rule and every disturbance. With real data
neither is available, so the counterfactual has to be reconstructed from other
information. The rest of the lecture is about how a regression does that, and
about what it has to assume.

A regression will not switch off one intervention; it pools many. Pooling forces
a choice that the table could avoid: how to date a gap.

## Two Clocks {#sec-l01-two-clocks}

A statement such as "the response at $t=7$ is 0.25" hides that choice. It could
be a fact about period 7, or a fact about what happens two periods after an
intervention. In the twelve-period economy the readings coincide because only
one intervention was switched off. They separate as soon as a second
intervention is considered.

### Calendar Time and Horizon

[**Calendar time**]{.glossary-term data-term="calendar-time"} $t$ is the date of
an observation: a quarter such as 1950Q3, or a period in a simulation. In this
course it also dates the intervention and, later, the regression row built
around it. The [**horizon**]{.glossary-term data-term="horizon"} $h$ counts the
periods after the intervention at which the outcome is measured, so $y_{t+h}$ is
read "the outcome $h$ periods after date $t$." The horizon is measured in the
data's own periods: quarters in the Ramey–Zubairy data and abstract periods in
the simulations. The opening's 1953Q1 is horizon 10 for news dated 1950Q3.

The response at $h=0$ is the
[**impact response**]{.glossary-term data-term="impact-response"}, the effect
within the period of the intervention. In the twelve-period economy it is the
gap of 1 at $t=5$. Horizons count upward to a largest horizon $H$ chosen by the
researcher: $H=2$ for the hand calculations of @sec-l01-rows-by-hand, $H=12$ for
the simulations, and $H=20$ quarters for the military-news data.

Now switch off the intervention at $t=10$ instead of the one at $t=5$, again
holding every $v_t$ fixed. The gaps at $t=10,11,12$ are 1, 0.5, and 0.25. On
the calendar these are new numbers at new dates. On the horizon clock they are
the same numbers as before: 1 at $h=0$, 0.5 at $h=1$, 0.25 at $h=2$. The rule
treats an intervention the same way whenever it arrives, so the gap depends on
the horizon and not on the date. That property is what allows a single sequence
$\theta_0,\theta_1,\dots$ to describe the response to every intervention in a
sample. It is an assumption about the economy, stated formally as
[A1](#assumption-l01-a1) below; if the effect of news depended on the state of
the economy, the response would carry a date as well, which is the subject of
Lecture 9.

### The Impulse-Response Function

The sequence of causal responses read as a function of the horizon,

$$
h\longmapsto\theta_h,\qquad h=0,1,\dots,H,
$$

is the [**impulse-response function**]{.glossary-term
data-term="impulse-response-function"}. It answers "how does the effect evolve
after the intervention?" with a curve rather than a number. In the twelve-period
economy the curve starts at 1 and halves each period.

The two clocks sort the objects of this course into two kinds. The realized
path of GDP after 1950Q3 is a function of calendar time and belongs to one
episode. The impulse-response function is a function of horizon and describes
what an intervention does whenever it happens. The rise of 7.87 points was a
calendar-time fact about 1950–1953. The policymaker's question was a
horizon-time question.

The distinction has a practical consequence. A regression that estimates the
response at one horizon returns one number, so it estimates one point on the
curve. Drawing the whole curve takes one estimate per horizon, and each estimate
uses its own rows of data, a fact that @sec-l01-rows-by-hand makes concrete.
Before estimating anything, though, we need to know what the curve looks like
in an economy where it can be derived rather than simulated.

## The Smallest Model {#sec-l01-smallest-model}

The twelve-period economy produced a gap that halved every period and ignored
the disturbances. Neither fact was an accident of the draws. Both follow from
the rule, and seeing why requires writing the rule with general coefficients.
The model we use is the smallest one in which an intervention has a response
that unfolds over time and in which that response can be derived exactly.

### An Autoregression with an Observed Shock

Let the outcome follow

$$
y_t=\rho\,y_{t-1}+\theta_0 s_t+v_t .
$$ {#eq-l01-toy}

Read @eq-l01-toy from left to right as a recipe for this period's outcome:
carry forward the fraction $\rho$ of last period's outcome, add $\theta_0$
units for each unit of the intervention, and add the disturbance $v_t$. A
series that equals a linear function of its own past plus new disturbances is
an [**autoregressive process**]{.glossary-term data-term="autoregressive-process"};
this one is first order, written AR(1), because a single lag of $y$ appears.
The coefficient $\rho$ measures
[**persistence**]{.glossary-term data-term="persistence"}, the share of any
deviation of $y$ that survives into the next period, and it has no units. The
coefficient $\theta_0$ is the impact response, in units of $y$ per unit of $s$.
The twelve-period economy is the case $\rho=0.5$ and $\theta_0=1$.

The intervention $s_t$ is drawn independently each period with mean zero and
standard deviation $\sigma_s$. The disturbance $v_t$ is drawn the same way, with
mean zero and standard deviation $\sigma_v$ measured in units of $y$. The two
sequences are independent of each other. Generated this way, $s_t$ is an
[**observed shock**]{.glossary-term data-term="observed-shock"}: a variable we
measure directly, that cannot be predicted from the past, and that is
independent of every other disturbance moving the outcome. In a simulation
this holds by construction. For the military-news series it is a claim, and
Lecture 3 examines what would make it believable. (The binary intervention of
the twelve-period economy has mean 0.3 rather than zero; a nonzero mean changes
only the regression intercept, as @sec-l01-model-to-regression notes.)

The derivations below use four assumptions. Each is stated once here and cited
by number where it does its work.

::: {#assumptions-l01 .assumptions}
[]{#assumption-l01-a1}**A1 (Linear, time-invariant dynamics).** The outcome
follows @eq-l01-toy with the same $\rho$ and $\theta_0$ at every date.
*Meaning.* An intervention of a given size has the same effect whenever it
arrives, and the effects of interventions and disturbances add up. *Used in.*
The forward substitution @eq-l01-forward, the response formula @eq-l01-theta,
and the date-free reading of the response in @sec-l01-two-clocks. *Without
it.* The gap between paths depends on the date, the state of the economy, or
the size of the intervention, so no single sequence $\theta_h$ exists; a
regression coefficient then averages different responses with weights the
researcher did not choose (Lectures 9 and 10). *Kind.* A modeling convenience
in the simulations and an empirical claim in data.

[]{#assumption-l01-a2}**A2 (Unpredictable intervention).** The interventions
$\{s_t\}$ are independent over time and identically distributed, with mean zero
and variance $\sigma_s^2>0$. *Meaning.* Nothing in the past, including past
interventions, helps forecast today's intervention, and the intervention
actually varies. *Used in.* The step $\mathbb E[s_tu_{t,h}]=0$ in
@sec-l01-model-to-regression, which needs $s_t$ to be unrelated to the later
interventions inside $u_{t,h}$, and, together with [A3](#assumption-l01-a3), the
step $\operatorname{Cov}(s_t,y_{t-1})=0$, which leaves $\beta_h$ unchanged when the
lagged outcome is dropped. *Without it.* If interventions are serially correlated, $s_t$
forecasts the later interventions in $u_{t,h}$ and its coefficient absorbs their
effects along with its own. Lagged interventions among the controls, as in Ramey
and Zubairy's specification, remove the part of $s_t$ that earlier interventions
predict, but they cannot stop $s_t$ from forecasting the interventions that
follow it. If $\sigma_s^2=0$ there is no variation to estimate from. *Kind.* An
identifying restriction.

[]{#assumption-l01-a3}**A3 (Independent disturbances).** The disturbances
$\{v_t\}$ are independent over time and identically distributed, with mean zero
and variance $\sigma_v^2$, and the whole sequence is independent of $\{s_t\}$.
*Meaning.* Whatever moves the outcome through $v_t$ neither causes nor is
caused by the intervention, at any lead or lag. *Used in.* The steps
$\mathbb E[s_tv_{t+j}]=0$ and $\mathbb E[y_{t-1}u_{t,h}]=0$ in
@sec-l01-model-to-regression. *Without it.* A disturbance correlated with $s_t$
is a common cause of the intervention and the outcome, and the regression
coefficient moves away from $\theta_h$; Lecture 3 derives the size of that
bias. If the disturbances are serially correlated but still independent of the
interventions, $\beta_h$ still equals $\theta_h$, but $\gamma_h$ no longer
equals $\rho^{h+1}$, because $y_{t-1}$ then also forecasts later disturbances.
*Kind.* Independence from the interventions is an identifying restriction;
independence over time is a convenience that keeps the control's coefficient
simple.

[]{#assumption-l01-a4}**A4 (Stationarity).** $|\rho|<1$, and the process has
run long enough that $y_{t-1}$ has the same distribution at every date.
*Meaning.* Deviations fade, and the averages that define a population
regression are the same whichever date we examine. *Used in.* Treating the
regression coefficients of @sec-l01-model-to-regression as constants rather
than functions of $t$, and the variance
$\operatorname{Var}(y_t)=(\theta_0^2\sigma_s^2+\sigma_v^2)/(1-\rho^2)$ used there.
*Without it.* The response formula @eq-l01-theta survives, but with $\rho=1$ a
response never fades and $\operatorname{Var}(y_t)$ grows with $t$; Lectures 2
and 5 study how estimates and standard errors behave as $\rho$ approaches one.
*Kind.* A mathematical convenience, and in data an empirical claim about
persistence.
:::

The twelve-period economy bends [A4](#assumption-l01-a4) slightly, because it
starts from $y_0=0$ rather than from a draw of the long-run distribution. The
larger simulations later in the lecture use a
[burn-in]{.footnote-term data-index="burn-in"}^[A burn-in is a stretch of
simulated periods that is generated and then discarded so that an arbitrary
starting value no longer matters. Starting from $y_0=0$ makes early outcomes
less variable than later ones: the variance of $y_t$ is its long-run value
times $1-\rho^{2t}$. The simulations draw 300 periods and
keep the last 200, and $0.9^{200}\approx7\times10^{-10}$.] of 100 periods. For
the hand calculations the start is harmless, since two paths that share $y_0$
have a gap that does not depend on it.

### Iterating Forward

We want the gap at $t+h$ caused by $s_t$. The model gives $y_t$ in terms of
$y_{t-1}$; substituting it into itself repeatedly expresses $y_{t+h}$ in terms
of $y_{t-1}$ and everything that arrives from $t$ onward.

The case $h=0$ is @eq-l01-toy itself. For $h=1$, write the rule one period
later and replace $y_t$ by @eq-l01-toy:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{t+1}&=\rho\,y_t+\theta_0s_{t+1}+v_{t+1}\\
&=\rho\bigl(\rho\,y_{t-1}+\theta_0s_t+v_t\bigr)+\theta_0s_{t+1}+v_{t+1}\\
&=\rho^2y_{t-1}+\rho\,\theta_0s_t+\rho\,v_t+\theta_0s_{t+1}+v_{t+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

One more substitution gives

$$
y_{t+2}=\rho^3y_{t-1}+\rho^2\theta_0s_t+\rho^2v_t+\rho\,\theta_0s_{t+1}
+\rho\,v_{t+1}+\theta_0s_{t+2}+v_{t+2}.
$$

The pattern is visible after two steps. Each substitution multiplies everything
already present by $\rho$ and appends the new period's intervention and
disturbance with coefficient one. After $h+1$ steps,

$$
y_{t+h}=\rho^{h+1}y_{t-1}+\sum_{j=0}^{h}\rho^{h-j}\bigl(\theta_0s_{t+j}+v_{t+j}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-l01-forward}

To confirm @eq-l01-forward at every horizon, argue by
[induction]{.footnote-term data-index="induction"}^[A proof by induction shows
that a formula holds in a first case and that, whenever it holds in one case,
it also holds in the next. Together the two steps cover every case.]. It holds
at $h=0$. If it holds at $h$, then
$y_{t+h+1}=\rho\,y_{t+h}+\theta_0s_{t+h+1}+v_{t+h+1}$ multiplies every term of
the formula by $\rho$ and appends the $j=h+1$ term with weight $\rho^0=1$, which
is the formula at $h+1$.

@eq-l01-forward is an account of where $y_{t+h}$ comes from. The first
term is the outcome just before the intervention, discounted by $\rho^{h+1}$
because it has had $h+1$ periods to fade. The sum collects every intervention
and every disturbance dated $t$ through $t+h$, each discounted by $\rho$ raised
to the number of periods it has had to fade. The newest arrivals count fully and
the oldest count least.

### The Response Is $\theta_0\rho^h$

Now run the counterfactual experiment on @eq-l01-forward. Remove a one-unit
intervention at $t$, and hold $y_{t-1}$, every disturbance, and every other
intervention fixed. Only the $j=0$ term of the sum changes, and it changes by
$\rho^h\theta_0$. By the definition @eq-l01-causal-response,

$$
\theta_h=\theta_0\rho^{h}.
$$ {#eq-l01-theta}

The impulse-response function of this economy starts at the impact response
$\theta_0$ and shrinks by the factor $\rho$ each period. Its units are those of
$\theta_0$, units of $y$ per unit of $s$, at every horizon. Because
[A1](#assumption-l01-a1) makes the rule linear, a two-unit intervention has
twice this response, and the response does not depend on the date.

Three checks confirm the formula. With $\rho=0.5$ and $\theta_0=1$,
@eq-l01-theta gives 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, exactly the gaps in
@tbl-l01-hand-table. No disturbance appears in @eq-l01-theta, which is why
changing the $v_t$ moved the realized path but not the gaps. And the limiting
cases do what persistence should: with $\rho=0$ the response lasts a single
period, as $\rho$ approaches one it barely fades, and with $\rho<0$ it
alternates in sign.

@fig-l01-persistence isolates the role of persistence. It holds the impact
fixed at $\theta_0=1$ and changes only $\rho$.

::: {#fig-l01-persistence}
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![](/lectures/01-question-to-projection/figures/fig-l01-persistence.svg){fig-alt="Two geometric decay curves start from the same value of 1 at horizon 0; the curve for rho equal to 0.5 is close to zero by horizon 5, while the curve for rho equal to 0.9 is still near 0.3 at horizon 12."}
:::
::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"}
![](/lectures/01-question-to-projection/figures/fig-l01-persistence.pdf)
:::
[Persistence sets the shape]{.smallcaps}. Both economies have the same impact response, $\theta_0=1$, and the same size of intervention. With $\rho=0.5$ the response has fallen to 0.0078 by $h=7$; with $\rho=0.9$ it is still 0.478 there. The difference comes entirely from the outcome's own persistence.
:::

With $\rho=0.9$ the response first falls below half of its impact value at
$h=7$; with $\rho=0.5$ it reaches exactly half at $h=1$ and falls below it at
$h=2$. In this model the intervention contributes only the size of the first
step. Everything after that is the outcome's own dynamics carrying the
deviation forward. A central bank's surprise and a war's news, if they hit the
same outcome with the same impact, would trace the same curve.

That conclusion depends on the single lag. An AR(1) can produce only geometric
decay, or an alternating version of it; a response that rises for several
periods before it falls, a hump, needs richer dynamics. The military-news
response in @sec-l01-first-contact has exactly such a hump. A method that
required the researcher to write down the correct dynamics before estimating
anything would be fragile for that reason, and the regression derived next
does not require it.

The derivation also used two things that data never provide: the rule itself,
and the freedom to hold every other term fixed while changing $s_t$. Data
provide rows of $(s_t,y_{t-1},y_{t+h})$. But @eq-l01-forward already writes
$y_{t+h}$ as a coefficient times $y_{t-1}$, plus a coefficient times $s_t$,
plus everything else.

## From the Model to a Regression {#sec-l01-model-to-regression}

In the twelve-period economy we found $\theta_h$ by rerunning the rule with one
intervention removed. A researcher with data cannot rerun anything. The move
available instead is to collect those rows for many dates $t$ and regress the
later outcome on the intervention and the earlier outcome. In the economy of
@eq-l01-toy that regression recovers $\theta_h$ exactly in population. The work
lies in finding which step makes that true.

### Estimands and Population Projections

Three objects need separate names. The
[**estimand**]{.glossary-term data-term="estimand"} is the population quantity a
procedure is meant to recover, fixed before any data are drawn; here the causal
estimand is $\theta_h$. A regression targets a population coefficient of its
own, defined next, which may or may not equal the estimand. An estimate is a
number computed from one sample, and it differs from the coefficient it targets
by an amount that changes from sample to sample. The notation keeps population
objects and estimates apart: population objects carry no hat, and estimates do.

The population object a regression estimates is a
[**population projection**]{.glossary-term data-term="population-projection"}.
For an outcome and a set of regressors that includes a constant, it is the
linear combination of the regressors with the smallest expected squared
prediction error, the
[best linear predictor]{.footnote-term data-index="best linear predictor"}^["Best"
means smallest mean squared error among all linear combinations of the
regressors. Setting the derivative of the expected squared error with respect to
each coefficient to zero gives the three conditions in @eq-l01-projection.
Ordinary least squares solves the same conditions with sample averages in place
of expectations.]. For the outcome $y_{t+h}$ and the regressors
$(1,s_t,y_{t-1})$ it is written

$$
y_{t+h}=\mu_h+\beta_h s_t+\gamma_h y_{t-1}+u_{t,h},
\qquad
\mathbb E[u_{t,h}]=\mathbb E[s_tu_{t,h}]=\mathbb E[y_{t-1}u_{t,h}]=0.
$$ {#eq-l01-projection}

The display has two parts. The first equation splits $y_{t+h}$ into a part
explained linearly by the regressors and a residual $u_{t,h}$. The three
conditions after it define the split: the residual has mean zero and is
uncorrelated with each regressor. Three conditions pin down three coefficients,
provided $s_t$ and $y_{t-1}$ both vary and neither is an exact linear function
of the other. The intercept $\mu_h$, the coefficient $\beta_h$ on the
intervention, and the coefficient $\gamma_h$ on the lagged outcome are the
numbers that satisfy them. The residual carries two subscripts because it
belongs to row $t$ of the horizon-$h$ regression.

The coefficient $\beta_h$ is a
[**projection coefficient**]{.glossary-term data-term="projection-coefficient"},
and it is what the regression targets. It is a feature of the joint distribution
of $y_{t+h}$, $s_t$, and $y_{t-1}$, and it exists in any economy with finite
variances, causal or not. A projection of next year's GDP on this year's
stock-market return has a coefficient, and nobody would read it as the effect of
stock prices on GDP without further argument. Whether $\beta_h$ equals the
estimand $\theta_h$ is a separate question, and the answer depends on the economy.

### The Forward Equation Is the Projection

The three conditions also give a way to find the projection: propose values for
the coefficients, compute the residual they imply, and check the conditions. If
the conditions hold, the proposal is the projection, because only one set of
coefficients satisfies them. @eq-l01-forward supplies the proposal. Matching it
term by term with @eq-l01-projection suggests $\mu_h=0$,
$\beta_h=\theta_0\rho^h$, $\gamma_h=\rho^{h+1}$, and a residual equal to
everything else in the forward equation:

$$
u_{t,h}=\sum_{j=0}^{h}\rho^{h-j}v_{t+j}+\theta_0\sum_{j=1}^{h}\rho^{h-j}s_{t+j}.
$$ {#eq-l01-residual}

Sort @eq-l01-residual by date. It contains the disturbances
$v_t,\dots,v_{t+h}$ and the interventions $s_{t+1},\dots,s_{t+h}$. It contains
nothing dated $t-1$ or earlier, and it does not contain $s_t$, which the
proposal has moved into the $\beta_h$ term. At $h=0$ it is simply $v_t$.

Now check the conditions one at a time.

1. *Mean zero.* Every term of @eq-l01-residual has mean zero by
   [A2](#assumption-l01-a2) and [A3](#assumption-l01-a3), so
   $\mathbb E[u_{t,h}]=0$.
2. *Uncorrelated with the intervention.* The product $s_tu_{t,h}$ is a sum of
   terms of the form $s_tv_{t+j}$ with $j\ge0$ and $s_ts_{t+j}$ with $j\ge1$.
   Terms of the first kind have expectation zero because the interventions are
   independent of the disturbances ([A3](#assumption-l01-a3)); terms of the second kind
   because interventions are independent over time with mean zero
   ([A2](#assumption-l01-a2)). So $\mathbb E[s_tu_{t,h}]=0$.
3. *Uncorrelated with the lagged outcome.* Iterating @eq-l01-toy backward writes
   $y_{t-1}$ as a discounted sum of interventions and disturbances dated $t-1$
   and earlier, a sum that settles down because $|\rho|<1$
   ([A4](#assumption-l01-a4)). Every term of $u_{t,h}$ is dated $t$ or later,
   and by [A2](#assumption-l01-a2) and [A3](#assumption-l01-a3) each such term
   is independent of everything dated $t-1$ or earlier. So
   $\mathbb E[y_{t-1}u_{t,h}]=0$.

All three conditions hold, so the proposal is the projection:

$$
y_{t+h}=\mu_h+\beta_h s_t+\gamma_h y_{t-1}+u_{t,h},\qquad
\beta_h=\theta_h=\theta_0\rho^{h},\quad
\gamma_h=\rho^{h+1},\quad
\mu_h=0.
$$ {#eq-l01-lp-toy}

@eq-l01-lp-toy answers the lecture's guiding question in its simplest setting.
The population regression of the outcome $h$ periods ahead on a constant,
today's intervention, and yesterday's outcome has a coefficient on the
intervention equal to the causal response at horizon $h$: under
[A1](#assumption-l01-a1)–[A4](#assumption-l01-a4), the coefficient the
regression targets and the estimand coincide. Running that regression separately
for each $h=0,1,\dots,H$ and collecting the coefficients traces out the
impulse-response function, one point per regression.
[Exercise 2](#exercise-l01-2) carries out the substitution for $h=1$ and $h=2$
and then in general.

A regression estimated horizon by horizon in this way is a
[**local projection**]{.glossary-term data-term="local-projection"}. In general
form, with a vector $\mathbf w_t$ of predetermined controls containing $p$ lags,

$$
y_{t+h}=\mu_h+\beta_h s_t+\boldsymbol\gamma_h'\mathbf w_t+u_{t,h},\qquad h=0,1,\dots,H,
$$ {#eq-l01-lp}

and the estimated response is the sequence $\hat\beta_0,\dots,\hat\beta_H$
[@jorda2005; @jordataylor2025]. In this lecture $\mathbf w_t=y_{t-1}$ and
$p=1$. The word [local]{.footnote-term data-index="local projection (name)"}^[@jorda2005
introduced the name. The method estimates "local projections at each period of
interest rather than extrapolating into increasingly distant horizons from a
given model," as a vector autoregression does. Because each horizon has its own
regression, errors in a model of short-run dynamics are not compounded at longer
horizons. Lecture 7 compares the two approaches.] refers to estimating each
horizon on its own rather than iterating one model forward.

### What Made the Coefficient Causal

The hand counterfactual changed $s_t$ while holding every other term fixed. A
regression cannot hold anything fixed. It compares outcomes across dates with
different interventions, and it succeeds here because of what $u_{t,h}$
contains. Across the many dates of a long sample, the disturbances and later
interventions inside $u_{t,h}$ are unrelated to $s_t$. Dates with large and
small interventions therefore differ, on average, only through $s_t$ itself; the
regression also adjusts for differences in $y_{t-1}$ that arise by chance. The
counterfactual is reconstructed from other dates rather than rerun.

That argument locates the causal content exactly. Steps 2 and 3 of the check
used [A2](#assumption-l01-a2) and [A3](#assumption-l01-a3); nothing about
regression did. Least squares would have returned a projection coefficient in
any economy. If the intervention were correlated with a disturbance inside
$u_{t,h}$, the same regression on the same kind of data would converge to a
number other than $\theta_h$, and nothing in its output would announce the
difference. Calling $s_t$ an intervention variable rather than a shock keeps
that possibility in view until Lecture 3 can address it.

The other two coefficients carry no causal reading. $\gamma_h=\rho^{h+1}$ is
the fading echo of the pre-intervention outcome, not a response to anything.
$\mu_h=0$ only because the interventions and disturbances have mean zero. With
the binary intervention of the twelve-period economy, whose mean is 0.3, the
intercept absorbs that mean and neither $\beta_h$ nor $\gamma_h$ changes. The
course reports intercepts and control coefficients but does not interpret them.

A long simulated sample confirms the algebra. With $\rho=0.9$,
$\theta_0=\sigma_s=\sigma_v=1$, and $T=100{,}000$ periods (seed 4), the
regression gives $\hat\beta_h=0.9985$, 0.9013, 0.8117, 0.6498, and 0.4249 at
$h=0,1,2,4,8$, against $\theta_h=1$, 0.9, 0.81, 0.6561, and 0.4305. The control
coefficients are $\hat\gamma_h=0.8990$, 0.8068, 0.7235, 0.5825, and 0.3792,
against $\rho^{h+1}=0.9$, 0.81, 0.729, 0.5905, and 0.3874. Every estimate lies
within 0.01 of its population value.

### Why Include the Lagged Outcome?

Condition 2 of the check never mentioned $y_{t-1}$. What happens, then, if the
control is dropped and $y_{t+h}$ is regressed on a constant and $s_t$ alone?

Nothing happens to the coefficient the regression targets. The omitted term
$\rho^{h+1}y_{t-1}$ moves into
the residual, but $s_t$ is uncorrelated with it, because $y_{t-1}$ depends only
on earlier dates. A regressor that is uncorrelated with an omitted term keeps
its population coefficient, so the projection of $y_{t+h}$ on $(1,s_t)$ still
has coefficient $\theta_h$ on $s_t$.

The residual, however, grows. Its variance gains
$\rho^{2(h+1)}\operatorname{Var}(y_{t-1})$. Under [A4](#assumption-l01-a4) the
variance of $y$ is the same at every date, so taking variances of both sides of
@eq-l01-toy gives
$\operatorname{Var}(y)=\rho^2\operatorname{Var}(y)+\theta_0^2\sigma_s^2+\sigma_v^2$,
or $\operatorname{Var}(y)=(\theta_0^2\sigma_s^2+\sigma_v^2)/(1-\rho^2)$. With
$\rho=0.9$ and unit variances, $\operatorname{Var}(y)=2/0.19=10.53$, and at
$h=0$ the residual variance rises from $\sigma_v^2=1$ to
$1+0.81\times10.53=9.53$. At $h=0$, $s_t$ is independent of every term in
either residual and neither residual contains a later intervention, so the
standard deviation of $\hat\beta_0$ in large samples is approximately the
residual standard deviation divided by $\sigma_s\sqrt{T_0}$. The regression with
the control has 199 rows, and the one without it can also use the first period,
which gives $1/\sqrt{199}=0.071$ with the control and
$\sqrt{9.53}/\sqrt{200}=0.218$ without it.

A Monte Carlo experiment checks the approximation in samples of realistic size.
Draw $R=500$ samples from @eq-l01-toy, each of 300 periods with the first 100
discarded, so $T=200$ (seed 3). In each sample run both regressions at every
horizon, then summarize the 500 estimates. @tbl-l01-control-precision reports
their means and standard deviations.

<!-- D2: the instructor build uses R = 500; students default to R = 200. -->

| $\rho$ | $h$ | $\theta_h$ | Mean, with $y_{t-1}$ | SD, with $y_{t-1}$ | Mean, without | SD, without |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.5 | 0 | 1.0000 | 1.0039 | 0.0730 | 1.0027 | 0.0946 |
| 0.5 | 4 | 0.0625 | 0.0523 | 0.1235 | 0.0552 | 0.1236 |
| 0.5 | 8 | 0.0039 | −0.0034 | 0.1234 | −0.0035 | 0.1229 |
| 0.9 | 0 | 1.0000 | 1.0040 | 0.0734 | 0.9666 | 0.2177 |
| 0.9 | 4 | 0.6561 | 0.6298 | 0.1978 | 0.6201 | 0.2693 |
| 0.9 | 8 | 0.4305 | 0.3973 | 0.2284 | 0.3979 | 0.2664 |

: Estimates of $\beta_h$ across $R=500$ simulated samples with $T=200$, with and without the lagged outcome as a control (seed 3; rounded to four decimals). Both regressions target the same coefficient, $\beta_h=\theta_h$; the control changes how widely the estimates spread around it. {#tbl-l01-control-precision}

At $\rho=0.9$ and $h=0$ the control cuts the standard deviation from 0.2177 to
0.0734, a factor of three, close to the large-sample values 0.218 and 0.071. The
gain shrinks as $h$ grows, because the omitted term $\rho^{h+1}y_{t-1}$ fades.
At $\rho=0.5$ it has essentially vanished after impact: at $h=4$ the added
variance $\rho^{10}\operatorname{Var}(y)$ is 0.003. The means sit near
$\theta_h$ but not exactly on it, and at $\rho=0.9$ the gaps are larger than
simulation noise. The regression without the control averages 0.9666 at $h=0$,
and the one with it falls short by 0.026 at $h=4$ and 0.033 at $h=8$. These are
small-sample biases, properties of estimates from 200 periods rather than of the
population coefficient, and Lecture 2 takes them up.

The control can be dropped without changing $\beta_h$ only because
[A2](#assumption-l01-a2) and [A3](#assumption-l01-a3) make $s_t$ unrelated to
$y_{t-1}$. An intervention that responds to past outcomes, such as a policy rate
set with an eye on recent output, breaks that link: dropping $y_{t-1}$ then
changes what the coefficient measures, and the control becomes part of the
identification argument. In this
lecture $y_{t-1}$ is there for precision; in most of the course controls do both
jobs.

@tbl-l01-notation collects the notation introduced so far. Each symbol returns
below where it does its work.

| Symbol | Meaning | Timing | Units |
|:--------|:--------------------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| $t$, $T$ | Calendar date of an observation and of a regression row; length of the series | — | periods |
| $h$, $H$ | Horizon; largest horizon estimated | outcome dated $t+h$ | periods |
| $y_t$, $s_t$ | Outcome; intervention variable | $t$ | units of $y$; units of $s$ |
| $y^{c}_t$ | Counterfactual path with one intervention removed | dates of $y_t$ | units of $y$ |
| $\theta_h$, $\theta_0$ | Causal response at horizon $h$, the estimand; impact response | $t+h$; $t$ | units of $y$ per unit of $s$ |
| $\rho$ | Persistence of the AR(1) outcome | — | none |
| $v_t$ | Outcome disturbance | $t$ | units of $y$ |
| $\sigma_s$, $\sigma_v$ | Standard deviations of $s_t$ and $v_t$ | — | units of $s$; units of $y$ |
| $\beta_h$, $\hat\beta_h$ | Projection coefficient on $s_t$, the regression's target; its least-squares estimate | row $t$, outcome $t+h$ | units of $y$ per unit of $s$ |
| $\mu_h$, $\gamma_h$ | Intercept; coefficient on the control $y_{t-1}$ | — | units of $y$; none here |
| $\mathbf w_t$, $p$ | Predetermined controls; number of lags they contain | dated $t-1$ or earlier | units of each control; lags |
| $u_{t,h}$ | Horizon-$h$ residual in row $t$ | disturbances $t,\dots,t+h$; interventions $t+1,\dots,t+h$ | units of $y$ |
