| $R$ | Number of Monte Carlo replications | — | count |

: Notation used in Lecture 1. $\mathcal T_h$ and $T_h$ are defined in @sec-l01-rows-by-hand. {#tbl-l01-notation}

The population regression is settled. A sample, though, contains a finite
number of dates, and the estimate depends on which of those dates had
interventions and how far each intervention was from the average.

## Why Many Shock Dates {#sec-l01-many-shock-dates}

The argument of the previous section averaged over "the many dates of a long
sample." The opening situation had, in effect, one. To see what a finite sample
can and cannot deliver, we look inside the least-squares slope and ask how it
uses each row.

### How a Slope Uses Its Rows

Take the simplest version first: the regression of $y_{t+h}$ on a constant and
$s_t$ alone, over whatever rows are available at horizon $h$. Write $\bar s$
and $\bar y$ for the means of $s_t$ and $y_{t+h}$ over those rows. The familiar
slope is $\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)(y_{t+h}-\bar y)/\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2$. Because the
deviations $s_t-\bar s$ sum to zero, the $\bar y$ term contributes nothing, and
the slope can be written as a weighted sum of outcomes:

$$
\hat\beta_h=\frac{\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)\,y_{t+h}}{\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2}
=\sum_t\omega_t\,y_{t+h},
\qquad
\omega_t=\frac{s_t-\bar s}{\sum_\tau(s_\tau-\bar s)^2}.
$$ {#eq-l01-ols-slope}

Read @eq-l01-ols-slope as a vote. Each row contributes its outcome, weighted by
how far its intervention was from the average. A row with an average
intervention has no say. Rows with unusually large interventions pull the slope
toward their outcomes, and rows with small ones pull it the other way. The
[weights]{.footnote-term data-index="regression weights with controls"}^[With
$y_{t-1}$ also in the regression, the same formula holds with $s_t-\bar s$
replaced by the residual from regressing $s_t$ on a constant and $y_{t-1}$ over
the same rows. That is the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell result, developed in Lecture 3.
In the AR(1) economy the residual is close to $s_t-\bar s$ in long samples,
because $s_t$ is unrelated to $y_{t-1}$.] sum to zero and satisfy
$\sum_t\omega_ts_t=1$, which are the two properties that make the slope ignore
any constant added to the outcomes and recover the slope exactly when every
outcome lies on a line in $s_t$.

Together, the two properties isolate the estimation error. Write the
outcome as $y_{t+h}=\tilde\mu_h+\beta_hs_t+\tilde u_{t,h}$, where $\tilde u_{t,h}$ is everything in
$y_{t+h}$ that the intervention does not explain; without the control, it holds
both $u_{t,h}$ and $\rho^{h+1}y_{t-1}$. Substituting into
@eq-l01-ols-slope and using the two properties,

$$
\hat\beta_h=\beta_h+\sum_t\omega_t\,\tilde u_{t,h}.
$$ {#eq-l01-estimation-error}

The estimate equals the population coefficient plus a weighted sum of
everything else that happened in the rows. When many rows carry interventions
of different sizes, and [A2](#assumption-l01-a2) and [A3](#assumption-l01-a3)
make those interventions unrelated to everything else, the weighted sum
averages toward zero. When few rows carry interventions, it need not.

The denominator of @eq-l01-ols-slope also says where the information comes
from. Row $t$ supplies the share $(s_t-\bar s)^2/\sum_\tau(s_\tau-\bar s)^2$ of
the variation the slope is estimated from. A sample in which a handful of dates
had very large interventions and every other date had none is, for the
purposes of this slope, a sample of a handful of dates. @sec-l01-first-contact
measures those shares in the military-news data.

### One Episode

Now push the argument to the opening's situation. Suppose exactly one row $\tau$
has an intervention, $s_\tau=1$, and the other $n-1$ rows have $s_t=0$. Then
$\bar s=1/n$ and $\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2=(1-1/n)^2+(n-1)/n^2=(n-1)/n$. The weight on
row $\tau$ is $(1-1/n)\big/\bigl((n-1)/n\bigr)=1$, and the weight on each other
row is $-(1/n)\big/\bigl((n-1)/n\bigr)=-1/(n-1)$. The slope is therefore

$$
\hat\beta_h=y_{\tau+h}-\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{t\neq\tau}y_{t+h}
=y_{\tau+h}-\bar y_{\text{others}}.
$$ {#eq-l01-one-episode}

Taken literally, @eq-l01-one-episode is the episode's outcome $h$ periods later
minus the average outcome $h$ periods after every other date. Substitute the
forward equation for the episode's outcome. With $\theta_0=1$ and $s_\tau=1$,
@eq-l01-forward gives $y_{\tau+h}=\theta_h+\rho^{h+1}y_{\tau-1}+u_{\tau,h}$, so

$$
\hat\beta_h=\theta_h+\Bigl(\rho^{h+1}y_{\tau-1}+u_{\tau,h}-\bar y_{\text{others}}\Bigr).
$$

The estimate is the response plus everything else that shaped that one episode,
measured against the other dates. The data contain one number, not two, and
nothing in them separates the response from the bracket.

The twelve-period economy puts numbers in the bracket. Keep only the
intervention at $t=5$: regress the realized outcomes on an indicator that equals one at $t=5$
and zero elsewhere, over rows $t=2,\dots,12$ at $h=0$. The ten other outcomes
sum to 9.636474609375, so their mean is 0.9636474609375, and

$$
\hat\beta_0=y_5-\bar y_{\text{others}}=-0.66875-0.9636474609375=-1.6323974609375.
$$

Since $y_5=0.5\,y_4+\theta_0+v_5=0.03125+1-1.7$, the estimate splits into
$\theta_0=1$ and everything else:
$-1.6323974609375=1+(0.03125-1.7-0.9636474609375)$. The disturbance of $-1.7$ in
the episode itself outweighs the response. The same calculation at $h=1$ and
$h=2$ gives $-0.984608$ and $1.512823$, against true responses of 0.5 and 0.25:
the wrong sign twice and six times too large once.
[Exercise 5](#exercise-l01-5) proves @eq-l01-one-episode and repeats these
numbers.

The Korean episode has the same structure, with taxes, the Accord, and price
controls inside its bracket. More episodes help only by averaging, and averaging
helps only if the other things are unrelated to the interventions across
episodes. If every quarter of war news also brought tax increases, adding wars
would not separate spending news from taxes, because the weighted sum in
@eq-l01-estimation-error would settle on something other than zero. That is the
identification question again, and it belongs to Lecture 3. What this section
establishes is narrower: a local projection is an average over every date with
variation in $s_t$, never a reading of one episode, and its precision depends on
how many dates carry that variation.

The formulas so far have treated "the rows" as given. Which rows enter a
horizon-$h$ regression is itself a calculation, and it is worth doing once by
hand.

## Building the Rows by Hand {#sec-l01-rows-by-hand}

A local projection needs the outcome $h$ periods after each date and, in this
lecture, the outcome one period before. Near the end of a sample the first does
not exist; at the start the second does not. The twelve-period economy is small
enough to list its rows for $h=0,1,2$ and compute every slope by hand, and those
slopes show why twelve periods cannot deliver the answer that @eq-l01-lp-toy
promises.

### Leads, Lags, and Regression Rows

A [**lead**]{.glossary-term data-term="lead"} of a series is its value $k$
periods later, $y_{t+k}$, and a [**lag**]{.glossary-term data-term="lag"} is its
value $k$ periods earlier, $y_{t-k}$. In a sample of $T$ periods the lead
$y_{t+k}$ is missing in the last $k$ rows and the lag $y_{t-k}$ in the first
$k$. In Stata the [time-series operators]{.footnote-term
data-index="Stata time-series operators"}^[After `tsset t`, `F2.y` is the
second lead $y_{t+2}$ and `L.y` the first lag $y_{t-1}$. Stata returns a
missing value whenever the requested date falls outside the data, and `regress`
drops every row with a missing variable without comment, so a horizon's sample
shrinks silently.] `F.` and `L.` construct them.

A [**regression row**]{.glossary-term data-term="regression-row"} of the
horizon-$h$ regression is one dated observation: the intervention $s_t$ and the
control $y_{t-1}$ at date $t$, paired with the outcome $y_{t+h}$. The row is
dated by the intervention, not by the outcome. Row 5 of the $h=2$ regression
holds $s_5$, $y_4$, and $y_7$.

The [**estimation sample**]{.glossary-term data-term="estimation-sample"}
$\mathcal T_h$ is the set of rows in which every variable of the horizon-$h$
regression is nonmissing, and $T_h$ is its size. Row $t$ needs the lag
$y_{t-p}$, which exists only for $t\ge p+1$, and the lead $y_{t+h}$, which exists
only for $t\le T-h$. Counting the rows between those limits gives

$$
T_h=T-h-p .
$$ {#eq-l01-sample-size}

<!-- D24: the droppable sample-by-horizon figure is replaced by this
     paragraph and the staircase figure. -->

Each additional horizon costs one row at the end of the sample, and each lag
costs one row at the start. In the twelve-period economy $T=12$ and $p=1$, so
$T_0=11$, $T_1=10$, and $T_2=9$, using rows $t=2,\dots,12$, then
$2,\dots,11$, then $2,\dots,10$. The count holds only when leads and lags are the
only source of missing values; @sec-l01-first-contact meets a case where the
data begin earlier for one variable than another. The regression without the
control could also use row 1, but we keep $t\ge2$ throughout so that the two
regressions use the same rows and differ only in the control.

@fig-l01-row-staircase shows the three samples.

::: {#fig-l01-row-staircase}
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![](/lectures/01-question-to-projection/figures/fig-l01-row-staircase.svg){fig-alt="Three stacked panels for horizons 0, 1, and 2, each showing twelve dated rows; the usable rows start at row 2 in every panel and end at rows 12, 11, and 10, and each usable row is linked to the outcome h periods later."}
:::
::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"}
![](/lectures/01-question-to-projection/figures/fig-l01-row-staircase.pdf)
:::
[Which rows enter]{.smallcaps}. Row $t$ pairs $s_t$ and $y_{t-1}$ with $y_{t+h}$, so each increase in $h$ removes the last usable row, and row 1 never enters because $y_0$ is not part of the data. The regressions for $h=0$, 1, and 2 use $T_h=11$, 10, and 9 rows.
:::

The staircase also exposes a detail that the population algebra handled
quietly. At $h=1$, row 4 has $s_4=0$, so it sits in the comparison group, yet its
outcome is $y_5$, which contains the intervention $s_5$. That is the term
$\theta_0s_{t+1}$ inside $u_{t,1}$ in @eq-l01-residual. In population it does no
harm, because $s_5$ is unrelated to $s_4$; in a sample of ten rows it is one
more source of noise in the comparison.

In Stata the three regressions are a three-line loop over the hand table:

```stata
import delimited using hand_table.csv, clear asdouble   // variables t s v y
tsset t
forvalues h = 0/2 {
    regress F`h'.y s if t >= 2
}
```

### The Slope as a Difference in Means

With a binary intervention, @eq-l01-ols-slope simplifies to arithmetic that can
be done by hand. Suppose $n_1$ of the $n$ rows have $s_t=1$ and the other
$n_0=n-n_1$ have $s_t=0$, and write $\bar y_1$ and $\bar y_0$ for the mean of
$y_{t+h}$ in the two groups. Then $\bar s=n_1/n$, and the denominator of the
slope is

$$
\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2=n_1\Bigl(1-\frac{n_1}{n}\Bigr)^2+n_0\Bigl(\frac{n_1}{n}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{n_1n_0}{n}.
$$

For the numerator, split the sum into the two groups:

$$
\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)\,y_{t+h}
=n_1\bar y_1-\frac{n_1}{n}\bigl(n_1\bar y_1+n_0\bar y_0\bigr)
=\frac{n_1n_0}{n}\bigl(\bar y_1-\bar y_0\bigr).
$$

Dividing the second display by the first,

$$
\hat\beta_h=\bar y_1-\bar y_0 .
$$ {#eq-l01-diff-means}

The slope is the mean outcome $h$ periods after intervention rows minus the mean
outcome $h$ periods after the other rows, and the intercept is $\bar y_0$.
@eq-l01-one-episode is the special case $n_1=1$.

In the hand table, @eq-l01-diff-means needs only group sums. At $h=0$ the rows
are $t=2,\dots,12$ and the intervention rows are
5, 10, and 12. Their outcomes sum to
$y_5+y_{10}+y_{12}=3.792626953125$, so $\bar y_1=1.264208984375$. The eight other
outcomes sum to 5.17509765625, so $\bar y_0=0.64688720703125$, and
$\hat\beta_0=0.61732177734375$. At $h=1$ the last row is 11, so row 12 and its
intervention have left the sample. The intervention rows are 5 and 10, whose
outcomes are $y_6$ and $y_{11}$: $\bar y_1=-0.06982421875/2=-0.034912109375$,
$\bar y_0=7.587548828125/8=0.948443603515625$, and
$\hat\beta_1=-0.983355712890625$. At $h=2$ the rows end at 10, the intervention
rows are again 5 and 10 with outcomes $y_7$ and $y_{12}$:
$\bar y_1=4.565087890625/2=2.2825439453125$,
$\bar y_0=1.62763671875/7=0.23251953125$, and
$\hat\beta_2=2.0500244140625$. @tbl-l01-hand-slopes collects the results.

```{=latex}
% A three-row table should not split: start a page if it would not fit.
\par\ifdim\dimexpr\pagegoal-\pagetotal\relax<0.42\textheight\newpage\fi
```

| $h$ | $T_h$ | Rows | Intervention rows | $\bar y_1$ | $\bar y_0$ | $\hat\beta_h$, no control | $\hat\beta_h$, with $y_{t-1}$ | $\theta_h$ |
|---:|---:|:---:|:---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 11 | 2–12 | 5, 10, 12 | 1.264209 | 0.646887 | 0.617322 | 0.575667 | 1 |
| 1 | 10 | 2–11 | 5, 10 | −0.034912 | 0.948444 | −0.983356 | −1.050405 | 0.5 |
| 2 | 9 | 2–10 | 5, 10 | 2.282544 | 0.232520 | 2.050024 | 2.153022 | 0.25 |

: Slopes computed from the rows of the twelve-period economy, rounded to six decimals from exact values. Without the control each slope is the difference in means of @eq-l01-diff-means; with $y_{t-1}$ included it is no longer a difference in means. {#tbl-l01-hand-slopes}

Stata's `regress` returns 0.61732179, $-0.98335569$, and 2.05002437. The
differences in the eighth decimal come from
[floating-point storage]{.footnote-term data-index="float storage"}^[Stata
stores a generated variable such as `v` in its default `float` type, which keeps
about seven significant digits, so 0.9 is held as 0.89999998. The file
`hand_table.csv` was generated that way, and its `y` column was computed from
the stored values, so exact decimal arithmetic and Stata's results part company
in the eighth decimal place. Reading the file with `asdouble` keeps
`import delimited` from rounding `y` to `float` a second time, which would
change the eighth decimal at $h=1$. Declaring both `v` and `y` as `double` when
the table is generated removes the gap.], not from the
arithmetic. Adding $y_{t-1}$ changes the slopes to 0.575667, $-1.050405$, and
2.153022, on the same rows. [Exercise 3](#exercise-l01-3) builds these rows by
hand, and [Exercise 4](#exercise-l01-4) reproduces them in Stata with
assertions.

None of the six estimates is close to its target. The impact estimate is 0.62
against 1, the $h=1$ estimate has the wrong sign, and the $h=2$ estimate is eight
times too large. @eq-l01-estimation-error explains why. With two or three
intervention rows, the weighted sum of everything else is dominated by a few
disturbances: the $h=1$ intervention rows have outcomes $y_6$ and $y_{11}$, and
$y_6$ carries half of $y_5$, with its disturbance of $-1.7$, while $y_{11}$
receives $v_{11}=-0.9$. The arithmetic of a
local projection is the same in a sample of twelve periods as in a sample of two
hundred. What changes is how many rows vote and how much of the noise their
votes cancel.

## Reading the Response Graph {#sec-l01-response-graph}

The hand table produced three numbers. A response is usually read as a curve,
and a curve raises two new problems. It needs one regression per horizon,
organized so that every coefficient stays attached to the rows behind it. And it
needs labels, because a curve by itself does not say what a unit of the
intervention is, what the vertical axis measures, or what the comparison is.

### From One Regression per Horizon to a Curve

Take one simulated sample from @eq-l01-toy with $\rho=0.9$ and
$\theta_0=\sigma_s=\sigma_v=1$: 300 periods drawn with seed 2, the intervention
drawn before the disturbance, and the first 100 periods discarded, so $T=200$.
The same 200 observations are shipped with the browser lab and the practicum,
so every medium works with identical rows. A loop estimates the response for
$h=0,\dots,12$ and stores each coefficient with its sample size:

```stata
import delimited using onedraw_rho09_seed2.csv, clear   // variables t s v y
tsset t
tempname P
postfile `P' h double beta_h T_h using results_onedraw, replace
forvalues h = 0/12 {
    quietly regress F`h'.y s L.y
    post `P' (`h') (_b[s]) (e(N))
}
postclose `P'
use results_onedraw, clear
assert T_h == 199 - h
```

Storing `e(N)` in the same `post` as `_b[s]` is what keeps each coefficient and
its row count together. The assertion checks @eq-l01-sample-size with
$T=200$ and $p=1$; if a missing value had crept into the data, the loop would
still run, and only the assertion would notice.
[Exercise 6](#exercise-l01-6) runs this loop and draws the graph, and
[Exercise 7](#exercise-l01-7) wraps it in a Monte Carlo experiment.

<!-- D32: the seed was fixed before any estimate was computed; the draw is kept
     although it is unusual at long horizons. -->

### What a Response Graph Must Say

A [**response graph**]{.glossary-term data-term="response-graph"} plots
$\hat\beta_h$ against $h$. Four pieces of information are needed to read it, and
the curve supplies none of them.

1. *The intervention and its units.* A coefficient is a response per unit of
   $s$, so the reader must know what one unit is. Here it is one unit of the
   simulated intervention, which is also one standard deviation because
   $\sigma_s=1$.
2. *The outcome's units.* The vertical axis is in units of $y$; in data it might
   be percent, percentage points, or points of trend GDP, and Lecture 2 shows how
   easily those are confused.
3. *The horizon unit.* The horizontal axis counts periods after the
   intervention, with $h=0$ the period of the intervention itself.
4. *The counterfactual.* The vertical axis measures the gap from the path without
   the intervention. A value of zero means "no different from that path," not
   "the outcome is zero" and not "the outcome is back where it started."

The intercept $\mu_h$ is not on the graph and is not the counterfactual path.
It absorbs means and says nothing about what would have happened without the
intervention. A complete caption fills the four slots and leaves the intercept
out; @fig-l01-one-draw is captioned that way.

::: {#fig-l01-one-draw}
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![](/lectures/01-question-to-projection/figures/fig-l01-one-draw.svg){fig-alt="Estimated responses from one simulated sample over horizons 0 to 12 lie below the true geometric response at every horizon and fall below zero after horizon 9, while a wide simulated 90 percent band surrounds the true response."}
:::
::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"}
![](/lectures/01-question-to-projection/figures/fig-l01-one-draw.pdf)
:::
[One sample against the truth]{.smallcaps}. Response of $y$ to a one-unit (one standard deviation) intervention $s_t$, estimated by local projections with $y_{t-1}$ as the control in one simulated sample of $T=200$ periods with $\rho=0.9$ (seed 2). Horizons are periods after the intervention; the vertical axis is the gap from the path without the intervention, in units of $y$. The true response is $\theta_h=0.9^h$. The band holds the middle 90 percent of estimates across $R=500$ simulated samples (stored simulation result, seed 3). This sample's estimates lie below $\theta_h$ at every horizon.
:::

The sample gives $\hat\beta_0=0.878940$, $\hat\beta_4=0.548477$,
$\hat\beta_8=0.240595$, and $\hat\beta_{12}=-0.293297$, against
$\theta_h=1$, 0.6561, 0.4305, and 0.2824. Every one of the thirteen estimates
is below its target, and from $h=8$ on the shortfall grows steadily, from 0.19
to 0.58. Read on its own, the curve says that the response turns negative after
ten periods. The true response is positive at every horizon.

The [5–95 percent band]{.footnote-term data-index="simulation percentile band"}^[At
each horizon, the interval between the 5th and 95th percentiles of the 500
simulated estimates. It describes how the estimator behaves when the true
economy is known. It is not a confidence interval, which has to be computed
from a single sample; Lectures 5 and 6 build those.] shows how unusual this
sample is. Across 500 simulated samples, 90 percent of the estimates at $h=8$
lie between 0.047 and 0.793, so a sample of 200 periods can deliver almost any
value in that range. This sample sits just below the band's lower edge at
$h=0$, stays inside it from $h=1$ through $h=10$, and falls below it at $h=11$
and $h=12$.
The seed was fixed before any estimate was computed, and the draw is kept
because its failure is informative: the errors at neighbouring horizons are not
independent. Adjacent regressions use almost the same rows, and
@sec-l01-residual shows that their residuals share most of their terms. When
one horizon's estimate is too low, its neighbours tend to be too low as well.

The same 500 samples also show where the estimates are centred. With
$\rho=0.5$, the mean estimate is within 0.014 of $\theta_h$ at every horizon.
With $\rho=0.9$ it falls systematically short: by 0.026 at $h=4$, 0.033 at $h=8$,
and 0.049 at $h=12$. The
[Monte Carlo standard error]{.footnote-term data-index="Monte Carlo standard error"}^[The
standard deviation of the estimates across replications divided by $\sqrt R$.
It measures how far a simulated mean could plausibly be from the mean that
unlimited replications would give; at $\rho=0.9$ and $h=12$ it is
$0.224580/\sqrt{500}=0.010$.] of those means is about 0.01, so the gap at $h=12$
is almost five times its standard error. It is the small-sample bias already
visible in @tbl-l01-control-precision, and Lecture 2 explains it.

The graph still lacks what a published response graph normally shows: a band
computed from the sample itself. The band in @fig-l01-one-draw used knowledge of
the true economy that no researcher has. A band built from one sample has to
start from the residual, and the residual has a structure of its own.

## What the Residual Contains {#sec-l01-residual}

The estimates in @fig-l01-one-draw erred in the same direction at every
horizon. The source of that pattern is visible in @eq-l01-residual once the
residuals of two rows are written side by side.

### Shared Terms Between Rows

Start with $h=1$. Row $t$ and the next row have residuals

$$
u_{t,1}=\rho\,v_t+v_{t+1}+\theta_0s_{t+1},
\qquad
u_{t+1,1}=\rho\,v_{t+1}+v_{t+2}+\theta_0s_{t+2}.
$$

The disturbance $v_{t+1}$ appears in both, with weight 1 in row $t$ and weight
$\rho$ in row $t+1$. Every other term is distinct and independent. With
$\theta_0=\sigma_s=\sigma_v=1$, the covariance of the two residuals is therefore
$\rho$ and each variance is $\rho^2+1+1=2+\rho^2$, so their correlation is
$\rho/(2+\rho^2)$.
Rows two periods apart share nothing, and their residuals are uncorrelated.

The reason is timing, not misspecification. The outcome of row $t$ is dated
$t+1$ and the outcome of row $t+1$ is dated $t+2$, but row $t$'s residual
reaches forward to $t+1$, into the period that row $t+1$'s residual also covers.
A regression of outcomes $h$ periods ahead on data sampled every period builds
overlapping windows, and overlapping windows share disturbances.

The same counting works at any horizon. For $1\le k\le h$, rows $t$ and $t+k$
share the disturbances $v_{t+k},\dots,v_{t+h}$ and the interventions
$s_{t+k+1},\dots,s_{t+h}$. A shared disturbance $v_{t+j}$ enters row $t$ with
weight $\rho^{h-j}$ and row $t+k$ with weight $\rho^{h-j+k}$, so it contributes
$\rho^k\rho^{2(h-j)}\sigma_v^2$ to the covariance. Summing these geometric terms
over $j=k,\dots,h$, and doing the same for the shared interventions over
$j=k+1,\dots,h$, gives

$$
\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(u_{t,h},u_{t+k,h}\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\rho^{k}\,\dfrac{\sigma_v^2\bigl(1-\rho^{2(h-k+1)}\bigr)+\theta_0^2\sigma_s^2\bigl(1-\rho^{2(h-k)}\bigr)}{1-\rho^2}, & 0\le k\le h,\\[2ex]
0, & k>h.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-l01-residual-acov}

At $k=0$ the first line is the variance of $u_{t,h}$. Read the formula from
the outside in. The factor $\rho^k$ discounts for the distance between the rows;
the fraction counts how much of the two windows overlaps, which shrinks as $k$
approaches $h$; and beyond $k=h$ the windows no longer meet. With
$\theta_0=\sigma_s=\sigma_v=1$ and $h=2$, the variance is $2+2\rho^2+\rho^4$ and
the covariances at $k=1$ and $k=2$ are $2\rho+\rho^3$ and $\rho^2$.
@tbl-l01-residual-ac turns these into correlations and checks them against the
residuals of a long simulated sample.

| Residual and lag | $\rho=0.5$, formula | $\rho=0.5$, simulated | $\rho=0.9$, formula | $\rho=0.9$, simulated |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $u_{t,1}$, lag 1 | 0.2222 | 0.2213 | 0.3203 | 0.3216 |
| $u_{t,1}$, lag 2 | 0 | 0.0019 | 0 | 0.0038 |
| $u_{t,2}$, lag 1 | 0.4390 | 0.4375 | 0.5914 | 0.5911 |
| $u_{t,2}$, lag 2 | 0.0976 | 0.0980 | 0.1894 | 0.1911 |
| $u_{t,2}$, lag 3 | 0 | 0.0011 | 0 | 0.0011 |

: Autocorrelations of the horizon-$h$ residual. Formula values come from @eq-l01-residual-acov with $\theta_0=\sigma_s=\sigma_v=1$; simulated values are the sample autocorrelations of least-squares residuals in one sample of $T=100{,}000$ periods (seed 4). {#tbl-l01-residual-ac}

<!-- D36: the residual is described as at most MA(h). -->

The residual of a horizon-$h$ regression is therefore correlated with its own
values up to $h$ rows away and uncorrelated beyond. In the language of time
series it is at most a
[moving average of order $h$]{.footnote-term data-index="moving average"}^[A
moving average of order $h$, written MA($h$), is a weighted sum of the current
and $h$ previous values of an uncorrelated sequence. Its autocorrelations,
the correlations of the series with its own values $k$ periods earlier, are
zero beyond lag $h$. "At most" allows for weights that happen to be zero: with
$\rho=0$ and $h\ge1$, for example, $u_{t,h}=v_{t+h}+\theta_0s_{t+h}$ is
uncorrelated with its neighbours.]. The correlation grows with the horizon,
because longer windows overlap more, and with persistence, because shared terms are
discounted less. At $h=20$, the longest horizon used with the quarterly data
below, the toy economy's residual is correlated with the residuals of the
twenty rows on either side. [Exercise 8](#exercise-l01-8) derives the
$\rho=0.5$ entries of @tbl-l01-residual-ac.

### Shared Terms Across Horizons

The same row's residuals at neighbouring horizons are linked even more tightly.
Comparing @eq-l01-residual at $h$ and $h+1$,

$$
u_{t,h+1}=\rho\,u_{t,h}+v_{t+h+1}+\theta_0s_{t+h+1}.
$$

The horizon-$(h+1)$ residual is $\rho$ times the horizon-$h$ residual plus one
new period. With $\rho=0.9$, most of what went wrong at one horizon carries into
the next. By @eq-l01-estimation-error, the estimation errors are weighted sums
of these residuals over nearly the same rows, so they inherit the link. That is
why the curve in @fig-l01-one-draw sat below the truth everywhere instead of
scattering around it: a response graph is not thirteen independent estimates,
and a pattern across neighbouring horizons can be a single error drawn
thirteen times.

### What This Does and Does Not Imply

<!-- D43: the paragraph below previews Lecture 5 in one labeled sentence. -->

Serially correlated residuals usually prompt a worry about standard errors, and
the worry is not wrong. But @eq-l01-estimation-error shows that what enters the
estimate is the residual multiplied by the intervention, not the residual
alone. Consider the products $s_tu_{t,h}$ and $s_{t+k}u_{t+k,h}$ for $k\ge1$.
The intervention $s_t$ appears in neither residual and not in $s_{t+k}$, it is
independent of all of them, and it has mean zero, so the expected product of
the two terms is zero. The products are uncorrelated even though the residuals
are not. Lecture 5 shows that inference on $\beta_h$ depends on the
autocorrelation of $s_tu_{t,h}$, which in this economy is zero because $s_t$ is
independent of everything else in both products and the control $y_{t-1}$ keeps
earlier interventions out of the residual, and it examines what changes when
either fails [@montieloleaplagborgmoller2021].

This lecture records the structure and stops there. The toy economy has done
its work. Beyond this point no known response is available to check an
estimate against, and the regression meets the data the lecture began with.

## First Contact with Data {#sec-l01-first-contact}

The opening asked what military news did to output. We now run the local
projection @eq-l01-lp on the quarterly data behind that question, with
$\mathbf w_t=y_{t-1}$ exactly as in the simulations: least squares of
$y_{t+h}$ on a constant, $s_t$, and $y_{t-1}$, one regression for each
$h=0,\dots,20$.

### The Data and Their Units

The data are Ramey and Zubairy's quarterly U.S. series for 1889Q1–2015Q4, 508
quarters, from the `rzdat` sheet of `RZDAT.xlsx` in their February 2018
replication package [@rameyzubairy2018]. The workbook's readme sheet is dated
November 21, 2016, and the package's `jordagk.do` describes the file as updated
April 7, 2016. The course does not redistribute the file: Practicum 01
downloads it from the authors' archive and verifies its checksum, and the
browser lab displays only estimates computed from it.

<!-- D5, D35: RZDAT.xlsx is acquired by script, never shipped. D33: the lab shows
     derived estimates only. D40: the units of newsy were checked against
     Ramey (2011, Table 2) and Ramey and Zubairy's documentation. -->

The outcome is real GDP divided by trend GDP, $y_t=\texttt{rgdp}_t/\texttt{rgdp\_pott6}_t$.
Both series are in billions of
[chained 2009 dollars]{.footnote-term data-index="chained dollars"}^[Chained
dollars measure real output by linking quantity changes between adjacent years
and expressing the result at a reference year's prices, here 2009. They make
GDP in different years comparable as quantities, though components measured
this way do not add up exactly.] at an annual rate, so $y_t$ has no units and
averages 0.987 over the sample. A change of 0.01 in $y_t$ is a change in GDP of
one percent of trend GDP.

The intervention variable is the military news,

$$
s_t=\frac{\texttt{news}_t}{\texttt{rgdp\_pott6}_{t-1}\times\texttt{pgdp}_{t-1}},
$$

the change in the expected present value of military spending announced in
quarter $t$, in billions of nominal dollars, divided by the previous quarter's
nominal trend GDP at an annual rate.
[Military news]{.footnote-term data-index="military news"}^[@ramey2011 built the
series from newspaper and magazine accounts of expected military spending,
recording the present value of each change in billions of nominal dollars; the
version used here begins in 1890 [@rameyzubairy2018]. Dividing by lagged
nominal trend GDP makes the news comparable across a century in which the
economy grew many times over. Lecture 2 discusses this scaling, and Lecture 4
uses the news as an instrument for government spending itself.] is recorded by
the quarter in which it arrived, which is why it is dated $t$ and the control
$y_{t-1}$ one quarter earlier. The series is nonmissing from 1890Q1 to 2015Q4,
504 quarters, and nonzero in only 108 of them. Its mean is 0.007222 and its
standard deviation 0.059728. The two largest values are 0.691893 in 1941Q4 and
0.600073 in 1950Q3. A unit of $s_t$ is news worth a full year of trend GDP, so
coefficients are best read per 0.01: news worth one percent of trend GDP.

Counting rows needs one adjustment to @eq-l01-sample-size. Row $t$ needs
$s_t$, which starts in 1890Q1, and $y_{t-1}$, which exists there because GDP
starts four quarters earlier. The lag therefore costs no row, and the
horizon-$h$ regression has $T_h=504-h$ rows, from 1890Q1 to $h$ quarters before
2015Q4. The formula counts a lag as a lost row only when the lagged variable
begins where the sample does.

### A Hump

The estimates rise from $\hat\beta_0=0.080313$ at impact to
$\hat\beta_4=0.259141$ and $\hat\beta_8=0.361906$, peak at
$\hat\beta_{10}=0.404210$, and fall back to 0.0796 by $h=20$.
@fig-l01-first-contact plots them.

::: {#fig-l01-first-contact}
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
![](/lectures/01-question-to-projection/figures/fig-l01-first-contact.svg){fig-alt="Estimated response of GDP relative to trend over horizons 0 to 20 quarters rises from about 0.08 at impact to a peak of about 0.40 at quarter 10 and declines to about 0.08 by quarter 20."}
:::
::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"}
![](/lectures/01-question-to-projection/figures/fig-l01-first-contact.pdf)
:::
[Military news and GDP, first contact]{.smallcaps}. Response of real GDP, in percent of trend GDP, to military-spending news worth one percent of the previous quarter's nominal trend GDP, from regressions of $y_{t+h}$ on a constant, the news, and $y_{t-1}$ over 1890Q1–2015Q4 ($T_h=504-h$). Numerically this is $\hat\beta_h$ per unit of the scaled news variable. Horizons are quarters after the news arrives. Read causally, the vertical axis is the gap from the path without the news, a reading this section lists as not yet argued. The response peaks at 0.404 at $h=10$. With Ramey and Zubairy's controls (four lags each of news, GDP, and government spending, both relative to trend), the $h=10$ coefficient is 0.294. No bands are shown.
:::

In words: news worth one percent of trend GDP is followed ten quarters later by
GDP about 0.40 percent of trend GDP above what the regression otherwise predicts
from the previous quarter's output. The shape is a hump, which @sec-l01-smallest-model
showed an AR(1) cannot produce, and the local projection found it without being
told what shape to expect.

Changing the controls changes the numbers. With Ramey and Zubairy's own set,
so that $\mathbf w_t$ in @eq-l01-lp holds four lags each of the news, of $y$,
and of government spending relative to trend ($p=4$), the sample becomes $T_h=500-h$ and the coefficients are 0.0510 at
$h=0$, 0.2938 at $h=10$, and 0.0671 at $h=20$. These equal, to the digits shown,
the linear GDP response in Ramey and Zubairy's replication code, which Lecture
4 reproduces. The peak falls by about a quarter. Which of the two
specifications deserves a causal reading, if either, is not a question the
regression can answer.

### Where the Variation Comes From

@eq-l01-ols-slope says that each quarter supplies the share
$(s_t-\bar s)^2/\sum_\tau(s_\tau-\bar s)^2$ of the variation behind the slope.
@tbl-l01-news-variation lists the six largest shares in the $h=8$ sample of 496
quarters.

<!-- D24: the droppable news-variation figure is replaced by this table. -->

| Quarter | News, fraction of trend GDP | Share of variation | Cumulative share |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1941Q4 | 0.6919 | 0.2612 | 0.2612 |
| 1950Q3 | 0.6001 | 0.1958 | 0.4570 |
| 1942Q3 | 0.4328 | 0.1009 | 0.5579 |
| 1950Q4 | 0.4022 | 0.0869 | 0.6448 |
| 1917Q2 | 0.3729 | 0.0745 | 0.7193 |
| 1941Q2 | 0.3401 | 0.0617 | 0.7811 |

: The six quarters with the largest shares of $\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2$ in the $h=8$ estimation sample, 1890Q1–2013Q4 ($T_8=496$). Shares use $s_t-\bar s$ as in @eq-l01-ols-slope; with $y_{t-1}$ in the regression, the exact weights use $s_t$ purged of $y_{t-1}$. Rounded to four decimals. {#tbl-l01-news-variation}

The quarter of Pearl Harbor and the first full quarter of the Korean War supply
45.7 percent of the variation in $s_t$ between them; four quarters supply 64.5
percent and six supply 78.1 percent. Of 496 rows, a handful carry the estimate.
The data are closer to the one-episode case of @eq-l01-one-episode than their
length suggests.

A direct test confirms it. At $h=8$ the estimate is 0.3619 on the full sample.
Dropping the single row for 1950Q3 raises it to 0.4340, so one quarter out of
496 moves the coefficient by 0.072. Dropping 1941Q4 instead gives 0.3443, and
dropping both gives 0.4451. Using only rows from 1947Q1 on, 268 of them, gives
0.0587. Removing Korea's news quarter *raises* the estimate: measured against
the regression's average, what followed the Korean news was smaller than what
followed the other large episodes. And most of what the full-sample coefficient
reports comes from before 1947.
[Exercise 9](#exercise-l01-9) reproduces the response, the shares, and the
drop-one estimate from the data.

### What Has Not Yet Been Argued

@fig-l01-first-contact is a response graph, and its caption names the
intervention, the units, and the counterfactual. It is not yet evidence about
what military news does to output. At least five claims stand between the
estimate and that conclusion, and each belongs to a later lecture.

1. *Units and transformation.* The outcome is a level relative to a trend
   fitted with data through 2015, and the coefficient is per unit of scaled
   news. Whether the level, the change, or the accumulated response answers the
   policymaker's question, and what units each carries, is Lecture 2.
2. *Controls.* One lag of $y$ was a choice. Ramey and Zubairy's controls lower
   the peak by a quarter, and which controls belong depends on what drives the
   news, which is Lecture 3.
3. *Identification.* The argument that equated the coefficient with $\theta_h$
   required the news to be an observed shock in the sense of
   [A2](#assumption-l01-a2) and [A3](#assumption-l01-a3): unpredictable from the
   past and unrelated to the taxes, monetary policy, price controls, and war that
   arrived with it. Lecture 3 argues about that, and Lecture 4 uses the news to
   estimate the effect of spending itself.
4. *Uncertainty.* No standard error or band has been computed. Overlapping
   windows make the residuals serially correlated, and Lectures 5 and 6 build
   intervals that respect what @sec-l01-residual found.
5. *Episode dependence.* Two quarters carry 46 percent of the variation, and
   dropping one moves the $h=8$ estimate by 0.07. Lecture 13 turns this into a
   systematic sensitivity analysis.

A sixth claim is hidden in [A1](#assumption-l01-a1). The regression treats news
worth 69 percent of trend GDP as having 69 times the effect of news worth one
percent, in slack and in booming economies alike; Lectures 9 and 10 ask what a
linear coefficient means when that fails.

## Handoff {#sec-l01-handoff}

The policymaker of June 1950 wanted to know what the buildup would do to
output. The lecture cannot answer that question yet, but it can now say
precisely what a local projection offers in reply. Each coefficient compares
what followed quarters with more news against what followed quarters with less,
holding the previous quarter's output fixed. In an economy where the news is an
observed shock, that comparison equals the gap between the realized path and the
path without the news. The coefficients are estimated one horizon at a time
from rows that shrink as the horizon grows. Their variation comes from every
quarter with news, weighted by how unusual the news was, and in these data a few
war quarters dominate.

The opening's evidence can now be set beside the regression. The realized rise
in output from 1950Q2 to 1953Q1 was 0.0787 of trend GDP. Scaling the $h=10$
coefficient by Korea's news gives $0.600073\times0.404210=0.2426$, three times
larger. Neither number is the effect of Korea's news. The first is a change
along one realized path, which @eq-l01-change-decomposition splits into a
response and everything else. The second applies an average over many episodes,
led by 1941Q4, to one of them, with controls and identification unargued.
[Exercise 10](#exercise-l01-10) asks you to take the comparison apart.

We can now produce a defined estimand, a derivation showing when a regression
recovers it, the rows of that regression listed by hand, a loop that estimates
the curve, and a response graph whose caption says what it measures. We cannot
yet defend a choice of the outcome's form. Every
regression in this lecture used the level $y_{t+h}$. The opening's 7.87 points
was a change, $y_{t+h}-y_{t-1}$, and @sec-l01-question insisted that a change
since the date before is not a causal response. Yet $y_{t-1}$ also sits on the
right-hand side of the regression behind every response graph we drew. If we
regress $y_{t+h}-y_{t-1}$ instead of $y_{t+h}$, is the answer different, or the
same answer in different clothes? Lecture 2 begins there.

## Further Reading {.unnumbered}

- @jorda2005 introduces local projections and argues for estimating each
  horizon directly rather than iterating a fitted model forward.

- @jordataylor2025 surveys local projections for applied researchers. Its first
  example, a Monte Carlo comparison of levels and long differences, returns in
  Lecture 2; Practicum 01 reproduces its levels curve at a reduced number of
  draws.

- @ramey2011 constructs the military-news series from narrative sources and
  explains why the timing of news matters for estimating the effects of
  government spending.

- @rameyzubairy2018 builds quarterly U.S. data back to 1889, with the news
  series from 1890, and supplies the data of @sec-l01-first-contact, which
  return in Lectures 2, 4, 9, and 13.

- @stockwatson2018 frames dynamic causal effects in macroeconomics and is the
  reading for the instrument conditions of Lecture 4.

- @montieloleaplagborgmollerqianwolf2026 compares local projections with vector
  autoregressions for applied macroeconomists and prepares Lecture 7.

- @inouejordakuersteiner2026 is the course's second standing reference, on
  inference for local projections, and is read from Lecture 5 onward.
